Quality checked lesson

First meetings often move from basic personal facts to interests and safe everyday topics. Names and greetings can also work differently in Japan, France, and Mexico.

Text to type: MATCHA shows how people introduce themselves at a first meeting by giving a name, where they come from, their work or school, and a hobby. A simple first meeting often has three layers: identity, interests, and easy connection. Identity includes a name, a place, and work or school. In Japan, a self-introduction is called jikoshoukai. A basic order begins with hajimemashite, a first-meeting greeting. The person then gives a name, where they come from, and their occupation. MATCHA uses Tanaka Miki as an example and includes student, company employee, and designer as occupations. The introduction can end with the polite close yoroshiku onegaishimasu.

MATCHA says that at school, mentioning hobbies or interests after an occupation can help classmates know someone more quickly. Typing practice

Type the text exactly. Timer starts with your first key.

Text to type: People do not greet one another in exactly the same way everywhere. In France, a cheek-kiss greeting is called faire la bise. It can be used among relatives or friends, but this does not mean that every first meeting includes a kiss. The custom also changes across the country. A popular French joke says that the city can be known by the number of cheek kisses because the number varies. Faire la bise is very common in southern France, even between male relatives or friends. In the north, it is less usual between unrelated men.

Typing practice

Type the text exactly. Timer starts with your first key.

Text to type: In Mexico, a title can be an important part of a respectful greeting. Titles are used with acquaintances, teachers, neighbors, shopkeepers, and people on the street. Na’atik explains that Don plus a first name can respectfully address an older man when his profession is unknown or he is not a professional. For example, Manuel Gonzalez can be greeted as Don Manuel. Teachers may greet each other as maestro or maestra without a name. These examples show that a first meeting may communicate respect through a title, not only through a plain first name.

Typing practice

Type the text exactly. Timer starts with your first key.

Text to type: After names and interests, people often move into small talk about everyday life. Small talk is polite conversation about small, safe subjects. It usually has a greeting, some conversation, and a closing. Its purpose is to build or keep a relationship, not to exchange important information. In English-speaking settings, common safe topics include the weather, sports, and television. Even “How are you?” usually receives a short, general answer rather than a detailed personal story. This final layer creates an easy connection while keeping private matters out of a new conversation.

Reading

Part 1: The Shape of a First Introduction

MATCHA shows how people introduce themselves at a first meeting by giving a name, where they come from, their work or school, and a hobby.

A simple first meeting often has three layers: identity, interests, and easy connection.

Identity includes a name, a place, and work or school.

In Japan, a self-introduction is called jikoshoukai.

A basic order begins with hajimemashite, a first-meeting greeting.

The person then gives a name, where they come from, and their occupation.

MATCHA uses Tanaka Miki as an example and includes student, company employee, and designer as occupations.

The introduction can end with the polite close yoroshiku onegaishimasu.

Reading

Part 2: Understanding Japanese Name Order

Name order is important because it can change with the situation.

In Japan today, people usually say the surname before the given name.

In Yamada Tarō, Yamada is the family name.

Yamada Tarō is also a common placeholder man’s name, like John Smith in English.

Yamada Hanako is the matching placeholder woman’s name, like Jane Smith.

In English, modern Japanese names have often appeared with the family name last.

However, JICE has used family-name-first order in its English documents since January 1, 2020.

Reading

Part 3: Hobbies Help People Connect

After identity, interests can help people find an easy connection.

MATCHA says that at school, mentioning hobbies or interests after an occupation can help classmates know someone more quickly.

Its example uses shumi, meaning hobby, and gives playing soccer as the hobby.

People can also share simple likes.

The page gives “I like sushi” and a stronger example about liking anime very much.

These small facts show what a person enjoys without giving private information.

Talking about hobbies can therefore move a meeting from basic facts toward friendly conversation.

Reading

Part 4: Greetings Can Change Across France

People do not greet one another in exactly the same way everywhere.

In France, a cheek-kiss greeting is called faire la bise.

It can be used among relatives or friends, but this does not mean that every first meeting includes a kiss.

The custom also changes across the country.

A popular French joke says that the city can be known by the number of cheek kisses because the number varies.

Faire la bise is very common in southern France, even between male relatives or friends.

In the north, it is less usual between unrelated men.

Reading

Part 5: Titles Can Show Respect in Mexico

In Mexico, a title can be an important part of a respectful greeting.

Titles are used with acquaintances, teachers, neighbors, shopkeepers, and people on the street.

Na’atik explains that Don plus a first name can respectfully address an older man when his profession is unknown or he is not a professional.

For example, Manuel Gonzalez can be greeted as Don Manuel.

Teachers may greet each other as maestro or maestra without a name.

These examples show that a first meeting may communicate respect through a title, not only through a plain first name.

Reading

Part 6: Moving into Safe Everyday Talk

After names and interests, people often move into small talk about everyday life.

Small talk is polite conversation about small, safe subjects.

It usually has a greeting, some conversation, and a closing.

Its purpose is to build or keep a relationship, not to exchange important information.

In English-speaking settings, common safe topics include the weather, sports, and television.

Even “How are you?”

usually receives a short, general answer rather than a detailed personal story.

This final layer creates an easy connection while keeping private matters out of a new conversation.
